title: AI job cuts at Bunnings, Qantas, NAB: ‘Mass unemployment is the business plan’
transcript:
Speaker 1: I'm Daniel James, and you're listening to 7am. This week, Bunnings announced hundreds of job cuts in a major AI overhaul. Last week, it was Qantas. Last month, it was NAB. Three giants of Australian business cutting jobs due to the growth of AI. The explanations were familiar. Bunnings says it will help deliver low prices for customers. Qantas says it will allow the airline to unlock innovation faster, while NAB says it's about reducing duplication and making the bank more efficient. We're told the AI revolution will make us more productive and more prosperous. What we're not told so readily is that mass job losses are part of the business model. Today, economist and co-CEO of the Australia Institute, Richard Dennis, on the rush to embrace AI and who stands to gain when workers lose their jobs. It's Wednesday, November 18. Richard, thanks for joining us. We're being told that artificial intelligence represents an enormous opportunity for Australia's economy, but some of our biggest companies are already announcing plans to cut jobs as they invest in AI. How are politicians and business leaders talking about the impact this technology will have on workers?
Speaker 2: Well, I don't think they're really talking about it enough. I don't think they're talking about it in the right way. And frankly, I don't know that they know what they're talking about. To be clear, the business model of AI is to cause mass unemployment. There is no secret about this. The whole idea is that companies around Australia and around the world will be able to sack hundreds of millions of people, replace them with AI.
Speaker 3: A well-known and respected tech CEO, Dario Amadei, who heads a cutting-edge AI company called Anthropic, is raising alarms tonight about AI's potential impact on employment that could soon be felt. He believes it could also lead to half of entry-level white-collar jobs disappearing and 10% to 20% unemployment in the next one to five years.
Speaker 2: And instead of spending billions on wages, spend billions buying AI services. And frankly, if that does not happen, then these big, powerful AI companies will be broke in a few years. So we really need to lean into the simple choice. We're about to cause mass unemployment or these AI companies are about to collapse because no one wants to pay them the enormous amount of money they need to recoup all the debt that they've already incurred.
Speaker 1: Yeah, I think Anthropic just posted an $ 80 billion loss for its last quarter, so that's how high the stakes are here. You've pointed out something interesting about all this, though. For decades, governments warned that moving too quickly away from coal and gas would cost Australian jobs. So why does the prospect of losing jobs seem to be treated so differently when it comes to AI? Yeah.
Speaker 2: The reason it seems so inconceivably incompatible, I would argue, is because politicians never cared about job losses. Certainly, the mining industry never cared about job losses. To restate it, for decades, we've been told we better not transition away from fossil fuels towards renewables because some workers in the coal and gas industry might lose their job. Come off it. You've sacked tens of thousands of public servants. You've privatized whole industries on the basis that would lead to job loss. Literally the same politicians saying we can't rush out of gas and coal because someone might lose their job are the same politicians saying we have to rush into AI even though it's going to cause mass unemployment. So the easy way to understand why it doesn't make any sense is they never meant it. Put simply, they've always been on the side of power. They've always been on the side of big companies. So when the fossil fuel industry didn't want to transition, we pretended to worry about the workers. Now that it's AI, well, guess what? We're on the side of the big AI companies. We were never on the side of workers.
Speaker 1: So does that speak to the power of the AI lobby if they're getting the same sort of reaction from proxies and potentially patsies within the parliament? to their lobbying?
Speaker 2: Absolutely. And this is what's unfortunate here. And there's a number of parliamentary inquiries going on at the moment. That's good. But I haven't really seen our parliament stand up and say, you know what? We're ultimately responsible for the well-being of Australia. We'll decide how fast AI is rolled out. We'll decide what the regulations look like. And perhaps most importantly, we'll talk about how to make sure that Australian citizens get some benefit out of this. I mean, it's really quite embarrassing to hear allegedly the most powerful people in our country, our parliament, talking about FOMO, talking about the fear of missing out and saying, well, we better give this big overseas industry what they want or we will miss out. And while the world is looking to us, we know it won't wait for us. If we hang back or stand still... this will just run right over the top of us. I mean, how embarrassing. We will miss out unless we stand up for ourselves. We will miss out unless we regulate and unless we tax. But instead of having that conversation, just like we missed out on the iron ore boom, just like we missed out on the gas exports, I'd suggest it's our rush to appease these foreign companies that will ensure that we will miss out on any benefits for AI. while experiencing all the costs.
Speaker 4: Business as usual outside NAB's Sydney office. But inside, a different story. Some 1,500 jobs will be gone by Christmas. Another 1,000 are set to follow by the middle of next year.
Speaker 1: Richard, last month NAB announced more than 2,500 drop cuts, citing amongst other things technological change. We've seen businesses including Telstra and the Commonwealth Bank invest heavily in AI. while talking openly about reducing the size of their workforce, how explicitly are these companies linking AI to job cuts?
Speaker 2: Oh, mostly they're being entirely explicit. And to be clear, after the National Australia Bank announced those job cuts, its share price went up. The reason that companies are being explicit about it is they're proud of it. They're saying to their shareholders, I've found a way to trim a billion dollars out of my wage bill and only spend $ 800 million on my AI bill, so we'll be $ 200 million better off, yay ass. This is my point. Mass unemployment is not an unintended consequence of AI. Mass unemployment is the business plan of AI. The job of a company is to maximize profit for its shareholders. This is capitalism.
Speaker 1: This is how it works.
Speaker 2: The only people who will stand up for Australians, hopefully our parliament, hopefully their unions, hopefully our local communities, and our parliament to date hasn't really facilitated an honest debate about, well, what are the benefits? What are the costs? But just as importantly, who will receive the benefits? Because if 100% foreign-owned AI company is picking up 99% of the benefits of AI.
Speaker 2: Then why are our politicians saying it'll be good for the economy? It might be good for GDP, but it's not going to help workers, it's not going to help consumers, and if all the shareholders are overseas, it's not going to help Australian shareholders. So unless they're paying a lot of tax, like the gas industry, there just isn't going to be anything in it for us Australians.
Speaker 1: Coming up, what we should be asking ourselves before we go all in on AI. Richard, there's an age-old argument, though, that we've been through technological revolutions before. Some jobs disappear, but new industries and better jobs emerge to replace them. Why aren't you convinced that that will happen again with AI?
Speaker 2: Oh, look, to be clear, as an economist and as someone who owns a smartphone, I am not anti-AI. I'm not anti-technology. What I am anti is our parliament and our public debate being rushed with FOMO rather than sitting back and actually evaluating what's being proposed here and what's not. The introduction of smartphones... was devastating for the Australian labor market. I mean, everybody my age, at least, will remember that actually to book a hotel room, you used to ring somebody. To book a flight, you used to ring somebody. Frankly, smartphones are much better at facilitating that booking than calling people ever was. But that technological change led to massive job loss as different companies said, well, you know what, we don't need four people sitting on the front desk waiting to answer the phone anymore. The introduction of tractors led to huge increase in unemployment amongst people who used to farm with shovels and hoes. I would much rather live in a rich country with productive tractors than thousands of people out in the heat literally digging in the soil. So technological change has always led to labor market change, and it always will. But unlike the smartphone, unlike the tractor, AI is potentially going to see massive job loss in a very short period of time, or it's a bubble. And either way, if we are going to rapidly shift tens of billions of dollars in wages into tens of billions of dollars in payments to American AI companies, that's going to have macroeconomic consequences, the likes of which we haven't seen in my lifetime.
Speaker 1: So Richard, what questions need to be answered before we jump headfirst into this as a nation?
Speaker 2: Look, there's a number of really simple questions that we should all expect really simple answers to. And until our politicians, until our business leaders can give us these simple answers, we should rightly be sceptical about some of these things. So As I said before, are we really expecting to see massive job losses in the next couple of years? If not, then what's all this FOMO? What's about to happen that we're being told we better not miss out on? Because usually with technology, you don't have to be the first person to buy the whiz bang new computer to kind of wait till they get a bit cheaper and you figure out which one suits you best. But we're being told we have to double down right now or we'll miss out. But if we're about to miss out, then something massive must be about to happen. Secondly, literally, who's going to benefit from this? So we're often told that AI might augment or support workers, and absolutely, it has that potential. But here's a simple question that no one's asked. If we're going to use AI in the health sector, is the government going to spend a lot more money buying AI support to sit on top of its current wages bill, or is are we going to shed lots of workers in the health sector to pay for the AI bill? Because it has to be one or the other. Either taxpayers are about to spend a fortune on AI and that expenditure is not in the budget, or we're about to shed a lot of workers to pay for the AI and no one's come clean about that. And then thirdly, When we talk about good for the economy, I really think that we need to break it down and say, which parts of the economy are we talking about here? Because if we spend $ 10 billion on wages in Australia, when those workers spend their $ 10 billion, it flows around the economy in predictable ways. But if we stop spending $ 10 billion on wages in Australia and spend that same $ 10 billion giving an American AI company $ 10 billion... Well, all of that money is going to slosh around the American economy. It's not going to slosh around ours. It's not good policy, and I think it's embarrassingly bad politics as well.
Speaker 1: And finally, Richard, you've argued that governments need to rethink what they're willing to regulate, what they're willing to subsidise, and what they're willing to say no to. So what should Australia be saying no to when it comes to AI, and what should we be subsidising instead?
Speaker 2: Well, let's be clear. If we let a whole bunch of AI data centers start up tomorrow, they will drive up demand for electricity. They will drive up everybody's electricity prices. When we wanted to tackle climate change with a carbon price, people panicked, industry panicked at the idea that electricity prices might go up. But now it's like, oh, come on, Richard, you're being a Luddite if you're worried about that. So We need to, in the short term, regulate how many and where data centers are built. We need to regulate where they get their energy from. I mean, you know, climate change still exists, according to this government. Data centers don't use special magical gas or special magical coal when they're using gas and coal to fund their enormous energy use. So we need to ask not just where the data centers are. We should regulate exactly what kind of energy they're using. And we should also be looking really hard at things like how we're going to protect copyright, how we're going to protect our democracy. Fake ads, I think, are a real threat to democracy. The idea that we're going to rush to approve and subsidise data centres that will then help flood our elections with fake images... I mean, talk about an easy way to kill a democracy. So we need to regulate the use of AI. We need to regulate where the data centers are located. And we're going to need to have a conversation about tax and benefits. We can't let this be another gas industry where we just let them set up, promising the benefits will trickle down to us. We need to know up front, sorry, what exactly will we get out of it? What are the guarantees for us? Not this FOMO that if we don't agree with them, we'll just miss out.
Speaker 1: Richard, thank you so much for your time.
Speaker 2: Thank you.
Speaker 5: Also in the news, the government has backflipped on plans to slash the number of backpackers eligible for working holiday visas. Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke had announced a cap of 5,000 third-year visas, but after pressure from the agriculture, tourism and hospitality sectors, that's now been upped to 25,000 places. The backpacker ballot system has also been delayed until next year. And a Queensland court has been played a phone conversation between fitness mogul Sam Wood... and his dad, where he asked to speak with his wife, suggesting that the domestic violence charges against him would be dropped if she recanted her statement to police. His lawyer denies the comments amount to a suggestion of interfering with the witness.
Speaker 1: I'm Ruby Jones.
Speaker 3: This is 7am.
Speaker 5: Thanks for listening.
